profiles.name: Tammy Grimes
profiles.excerpt: Tammy Grimes brought an unmistakable stage voice to CBS Radio Mystery Theater, first as an actress and finally as the anthology’s last host after E. G. Marshall.
profiles.bio_html:
Tammy Grimes built her reputation on the New York stage, winning a Tony Award for The Unsinkable Molly Brown and developing a voice and comic presence that were difficult to confuse with anyone else’s. Radio became an important later chapter rather than the foundation of her career.

Grimes appeared repeatedly on CBS Radio Mystery Theater, including the five-part Nefertiti cycle, before producer Himan Brown chose her to succeed E. G. Marshall as host in 1982. The change mattered because the host was the only continuing personality in an anthology whose casts and stories changed nightly. Grimes did not imitate Marshall; she made the creaking-door ritual her own.

Golden Radio Hour’s current index preserves 13 host/performer-tagged CBS Radio Mystery Theater appearances, while external episode guides document a larger acting and hosting record. GRH therefore classifies her as both performer and host rather than treating those final broadcasts as ordinary acting roles.

profiles.name: Ramsay Hill
profiles.excerpt: Ramsay Hill brought military experience, languages and stage discipline into a long radio career that included major NBC University Theater narration and literary roles.
profiles.bio_html:
Ramsay Hill was born Cyril Seys Ramsay-Hill in British Guiana in 1889 and had a life before acting that was unusually useful to Hollywood. He studied chemistry, served in the Royal Buckinghamshire Hussars during the First World War and later worked as a military technical adviser and dialogue coach as well as an actor.

Radio gave Hill more substantial dramatic opportunities than many of his often-small film parts. His credits included literary adaptations, anthology drama and narration, with roles ranging from Poe and Wilkie Collins to the title part in NBC University Theater’s The Old General. His military background and precise diction also made him credible in authoritative or historical material.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 24 NBC University Theater narrator/performer credits, 18 Escape performances and additional work on Suspense, Lux Radio Theatre, Screen Directors Playhouse and other series. GRH keeps him distinct from his son John Ramsay Hill, who also had a radio career.

profiles.name: Lamont Johnson
profiles.excerpt: Lamont Johnson learned broadcasting as a teenage radio actor and announcer before becoming one of television’s most respected directors, carrying lessons from live sound drama into visual storytelling.
profiles.bio_html:
Lamont Johnson began in radio while still a teenager. Raised in Pasadena, he performed in radio drama, worked as a local announcer and disc jockey and later became a network actor. His radio roles included Archie Goodwin opposite Sydney Greenstreet’s Nero Wolfe and the title role in a syndicated Tarzan series.

GRH’s archive captures the overlap between acting and announcing. Johnson announced or narrated programs including This Is Your FBI, The Whistler, The Six Shooter, Tales of the Texas Rangers and Words at War while also appearing as a character actor. He later moved decisively into television direction, winning Emmys and Directors Guild awards for work that often centered on difficult social or moral choices.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 14 This Is Your FBI announcer/performer credits, nine Broadway Is My Beat performances, seven Whistler announcer/performer credits, six Six Shooter announcer/performer credits and additional narration elsewhere. Radio was therefore not a footnote but the training ground for his later directing career.

profiles.name: Frank Knight
profiles.excerpt: Frank Knight was the announcer who framed Murder Clinic’s rotating gallery of fictional detectives, while also remaining active as a dramatic radio actor.
profiles.bio_html:
Frank Knight’s clearest announcing work in the GRH record is Murder Clinic, the Mutual anthology that changed detectives from week to week. The announcer’s opening had to explain the unusual format quickly, introduce that night’s featured sleuth and move listeners into the story without a continuing star to do the work.

Surviving scripts identify Knight by name in that role, including the 1942 broadcast “The Scrap of Lace.” He also appeared as an actor on other dramatic programs, showing the same kind of repertory flexibility common among New York radio professionals.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves three Murder Clinic announcer credits plus performances on Have Gun, Will Travel, I Love a Mystery and Gunsmoke. The surviving personal record is thin, so GRH centers the page on the verified announcing function rather than inventing a larger biography.

profiles.name: Roger De Koven
profiles.excerpt: Roger De Koven was a durable New York radio actor whose long serial career also included formal narration, from O. Henry dramatizations to science fiction.
profiles.bio_html:
Roger De Koven built a broad radio career during the years when New York actors could work across serials, anthology drama and narration in the same week. He held continuing roles on programs including Myrt and Marge, The O’Neills, Against the Storm and Stella Dallas, giving him experience with both daily continuity and self-contained drama.

De Koven was also used as a narrator, notably on Famous O. Henry Jury Trials. Later anthology work continued that blend of character and narrative authority, including science-fiction programs where narration often had to establish unfamiliar settings with very little time.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 12 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances, nine The Chase, six X Minus One narrator/performer credits and additional work on The Mysterious Traveler, Theater Five, CBS Radio Workshop and other series. GRH therefore keeps narration as a meaningful secondary facet of his long radio career.

profiles.name: William Lally
profiles.excerpt: William Lally was a West Coast repertory actor who also handled announcing duties on Philip Marlowe and Gunsmoke, moving between continuity and character work inside dramatic radio.
profiles.bio_html:
William Lally is better documented through program credits than through personal publicity. His GRH record shows a working West Coast radio actor appearing in literary drama, westerns and detective programs while also taking on announcing assignments.

That dual use is clearest on The Adventures of Philip Marlowe, where Lally is credited as announcer and performer, and on Gunsmoke, where the same overlap appears. In a dramatic series, the announcer had to maintain sponsor and network continuity while the actor had to vanish into the fictional world, making the combination a useful measure of professional versatility.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves nine NBC University Theater performances, six Philip Marlowe announcer/performer credits, three Sears Radio Theater appearances and smaller credits on Gunsmoke, Escape, Frontier Gentleman and Night Beat. GRH keeps the profile grounded in that documented work.

profiles.name: John Larkin
profiles.excerpt: John Larkin carried the discipline of daytime serial acting into anthology narration and science fiction, long before television audiences knew him from The Edge of Night.
profiles.bio_html:
John Larkin became one of radio’s experienced serial actors, spending years in daytime drama before television brought him wider recognition. That daily work demanded continuity, vocal control and the ability to make exposition sound spontaneous, skills that transferred naturally to anthology narration.

Golden Radio Hour’s strongest surviving Larkin record is in X Minus One, where he appears in both narrator and performer roles. The series often needed voices that could explain speculative premises quickly without making them sound like lectures, and Larkin’s soap-opera training made him well suited to that task.

GRH currently preserves 13 X Minus One narrator/performer credits, three John Steele, Adventurer performances and additional work on Gang Busters, Columbia Workshop, Dimension X and The Chase. His page therefore recognizes narration as one facet of a much broader radio acting career.

profiles.name: Frank Martin
profiles.excerpt: Frank Martin’s voice was part of the architecture of Lights Out, where he announced Arch Oboler’s supernatural drama and delivered sponsor copy without breaking the program’s carefully built mood.
profiles.bio_html:
Frank Martin is most clearly documented in GRH as an announcer and commercial spokesman rather than as a star actor. His strongest association is with Arch Oboler’s Lights Out, a program whose openings deliberately warned listeners about the disturbing stories ahead before sliding into sponsor material.

Surviving scripts identify Martin directly as announcer and place him in the commercial transitions for Ironized Yeast. That job required a delicate shift: the sponsor message had to remain intelligible and persuasive without puncturing the ominous atmosphere Oboler had just established.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 21 Lights Out announcer/commercial-spokesman credits, six Tales of the Texas Rangers commercial-spokesman/performer credits and additional announcing or commercial work on The Halls of Ivy, Dangerous Assignment and I Love a Mystery. GRH therefore tags both announcing and sponsor performance as genuine parts of his radio career.

profiles.name: Junius Matthews
profiles.excerpt: Junius Matthews was a veteran stage and radio character actor whose warm, distinctive voice ranged from western old-timers and announcing work to Disney’s Rabbit and Archimedes.
profiles.bio_html:
Junius Matthews began on Broadway before the First World War and worked across stage, silent film, radio, television and animation for more than half a century. Radio made particular use of his distinctive, slightly reedy character voice, often casting him as older men, frontier eccentrics and supporting figures.

His radio career included the Tin Woodsman in a broadcast version of The Wizard of Oz, Wichita on Luke Slaughter of Tombstone and extensive supporting work in western and detective drama. GRH also preserves a large set of announcing credits on Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, showing that the same recognizable voice could function outside character roles.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 50 Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar announcer/performer credits, ten Luke Slaughter of Tombstone performances, nine Philip Marlowe appearances and additional work on Broadway Is My Beat, The Line Up and Escape. Later audiences heard Matthews as Rabbit in Disney’s Winnie the Pooh films and Archimedes in The Sword in the Stone.
